bull_thesis: Everforth (formerly ASGN) is a genuinely cash-generative technology-services franchise trading at a value multiple after a brutal de-rating. On a sum-of-the-parts basis (valuing each business line separately), the Commercial business (about $2.79B of revenue, 70% of the total, shifting toward higher-margin consulting now roughly 63% of sales) and the Federal Government business (about $1.19B, backed by $2.8-3.1B of contract backlog and a defense-budget tailwind from the One Big Beautiful Bill) together throw off around $380M of adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) and about $221M of trailing-twelve-month free cash flow. At today's roughly $28 the enterprise (equity plus roughly $1.39B of net debt) is valued near 6.6x EBITDA and the equity near 5x free cash flow - a clear discount to federal IT-services peers even after those peers themselves de-rated. The load-bearing evidence that the story is turning arrived on 29 July 2026: second-quarter revenue rose to $1.007B, adjusted EBITDA margin recovered to 9.6% from a weak 8.6% in the first quarter, and earnings beat consensus ($0.91 versus $0.81). Management is returning capital (a $1B buyback already in use, $64M in Q4-25 and 0.4M shares in Q2-26), refinanced and upsized its revolver to 2031, and open-market insider buying (17 buys versus 11 sells) signals real conviction. If the consulting mix-shift and offshore India delivery (via the Quinnox acquisition) restore margins toward the 11% the business ran in late 2025, normalized earnings power near $2.50-3.00 per share at a modest 12-13x supports the mid-$30s to low-$40s, with buybacks shrinking the share count as an added lever. Conditions that must hold: margins keep climbing back, federal bookings recover from the 0.7x book-to-bill trough, and revenue at least stabilizes.
bear_thesis: This is a slowly shrinking, levered business whose cheapness may be a value trap, and the easy money has already been made. Revenue has fallen four straight years - from $4.58B in 2022 to $3.98B in 2025 - and earnings per share have more than halved, from $5.23 to $2.60, with trailing-twelve-month earnings now just $1.94. The core threat is structural: staff-augmentation and even routine consulting are exactly the billable IT labor that AI coding tools and offshore arbitrage deflate. Management's whole pivot - rebrand to Everforth, offshore India delivery, AI accelerators, and a reporting change that conveniently hides the staffing-versus-consulting split - is a defensive response to that erosion, not offense. The balance sheet compounds the risk: net debt near $1.39B is roughly 3.5x EBITDA, and the Altman-Z solvency score of 1.7 sits in the caution band. The first-quarter 2026 margin miss (8.6%, below management's own guide) showed how quickly profitability can crack, and analysts have pushed repeatedly on whether the softness is structural pricing pressure rather than the 'timing and mix' management insists on. Critically, the stock has already re-rated about 55% off its mid-July low near $17-18 to roughly $28 on the Q2 print; the margin-recovery catalyst is largely spent. At today's price the discount to a defensible mid-$30s value is modest, and if margins stall or revenue keeps sliding, fair value drifts back toward the low-$20s. consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power - and the answer here is: not anymore. forcing_function: There is no discrete hard date or corporate event that forces a re-rating from here - which is the core reason this is a wait-for-a-better-entry call rather than an enter-now one. # Everforth, Inc. (EFOR, formerly ASGN Incorporated) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Coverage window: five consecutive quarterly
calls, first quarter 2025 through first quarter 2026 (the final call under the ASGN
name), supplemented by the second-quarter 2026 results released 29 July 2026. Everforth
is a US technology and digital-engineering services firm with two segments: a Commercial
business (about 70% of revenue) serving Fortune-1000 clients, and a Federal Government
business (about 30%) serving the Department of Defense, the intelligence community and
civilian agencies.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has quietly changed shape. In early 2025 management sold a familiar idea: an
IT-staffing and services model that is "resilient across economic cycles," steadied by a
variable cost base, with a slow, favorable drift toward higher-margin consulting
(consulting revenue rose from 57% of the total in early 2024 to roughly 63% by late
2025). Over the following year that arc widened into a full re-invention: a string of
acquisitions (TopBloc and GlideFast in the Workday/ServiceNow orbit, then Quinnox for
offshore delivery in India), a bundle of new "AI accelerator" assets, a fresh senior
leadership bench, and finally a complete corporate rebrand — ASGN became Everforth in
February 2026, with the ticker moving to EFOR that April.

Two drivers were introduced with fanfare and are worth watching. First, "AI-led
transformation" became the dominant demand narrative — by the fourth-quarter 2025 call
management claimed "nearly 80% of enterprises" plan to lift AI spending in 2026. Second,
offshore India delivery (via Quinnox) was framed as the route to margin expansion. A
driver that was quietly de-emphasized: the staff-augmentation business itself. Alongside
the rebrand, management changed its commercial reporting from "mode of delivery"
(staffing versus consulting) to "by industry" — a change that, whatever its intent,
removes the very disclosure investors had used to track the decline of the legacy
staffing base.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The recurring tension is a confident bookings narrative sitting on top of a shrinking
revenue line.

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record commercial consulting bookings," book-to-bill 1.1–1.3x (every quarter) | Total revenue fell each year: $4.58B (2022) → $4.45B (2023) → $4.10B (2024) → $3.98B (2025); Q1-26 flat year on year | Bookings strength is real but is NOT converting to revenue growth — management conceded in Q1-26 that project "ramp-up time was slower than anticipated" |
| Margins "creeping up... adding to our margin profile" (Q2-25 CEO) | Adjusted EBITDA margin then MISSED in Q1-26 at 8.6%, "below our expectations"; full-year EPS collapsed from $3.83 (2024) to $2.60 (2025), and trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS is now just $1.94; net margin only 2.9% | The margin-up story broke in Q1-26 before partially healing in Q2-26 (9.6%) |
| "Disciplined capital allocation... strength of our balance sheet" | Net debt is about $1.39B against roughly $380M of adjusted EBITDA — leverage near 3.5x; the Altman-Z solvency score of 1.7 sits in the caution/distress band | The balance sheet is levered, not pristine — though they DID refinance and upsize the revolver to $600M out to 2031 (July 2026) and are buying back stock |
| AI is a demand tailwind | Revenue is still shrinking while AI adoption accelerates — the same technology that drives modernization projects also deflates the billable-labor base | Two-sided; the tailwind is real for consulting demand but does not yet offset the secular pressure on the staffing model |

The cleanest corroboration of management's better claims: free cash flow is genuine —
about $221M on a trailing-twelve-month basis, converting roughly 60–68% of EBITDA, and
Q4-25 alone produced $93.7M. This is a real cash business, not an accounting mirage.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining through 2025, then stabilizing.** Rating: Declining-to-turning.

- Q1-25: cautious but steady — management widened guidance ranges, citing "a new piece
  of news almost daily... tariffs or DOGE," framed as "just good caution."
- Q2–Q3-25: the most offensive tone of the window — "AI is not merely a passing fad but a
  fundamental replatforming," record commercial bookings, the One Big Beautiful Bill
  defense-budget tailwind.
- Q4-25/Q1-26: distinctly defensive — "very volatile macro environment," "disciplined
  expense management," and the admission of an EBITDA-margin miss. The language shifted
  from growth and investment toward cost control and "strengthening our foundation."
- Q2-26 (July): a modest confidence rebound on the earnings beat and margin recovery.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** Management is reliable on the top line and less so on margin. Through 2025
revenue repeatedly landed "at" or "above the high end" of guidance, and Q2-26 revenue and
EPS both beat consensus (EPS $0.91 versus $0.81 expected). But the Q1-26 adjusted-EBITDA
margin of 8.6% came in below management's own expectation — a genuine miss on the metric
that matters most to this thesis. The screener's beat rate of four of the last seven
quarters (57%) is consistent with a "usually hits, occasionally stumbles" profile. No
strong sandbagging pattern; if anything the margin guide has been slightly optimistic.
Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Two questions recur and are never fully put to bed. Surinder Thind (of the sell side)
pressed quarter after quarter on the true go-forward margin run-rate and on financial-
services weakness — and in Q1-26 that pressure was vindicated when margins missed. Mark
Marcon repeatedly probed whether the margin compression reflected pricing pressure or
mere mix; management insisted "we're not seeing a material compression in pricing... it
was really timing" and "mix." That deflection is the single most important claim to
distrust: if the softness is structural pricing rather than temporary mix, the recovery
management promises "gradually throughout the year, won't rubber-band it" may not arrive.
Marcon also pushed on days-sales-outstanding and free-cash-flow conversion; management
attributed it to seasonality with "no change in behavior, no increase in bad debt."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Revenue has declined four consecutive years and earnings per share have more than
halved from the 2022 peak. 🔴 The Q1-26 margin miss, with federal book-to-bill sliding to
0.7x that quarter. 🔴 Leverage near 3.5x with an Altman-Z of 1.7. 🔴 Analyst price-target
velocity is down about 37% versus the year-ago average, and a plaintiff law firm
(Johnson Fistel) publicized a securities-law "investigation" in May 2026 — boilerplate
that follows any large drawdown, but worth noting. 🔴 The reporting change that hides the
staffing-versus-consulting split.

🟢 Q2-26 delivered the first hard evidence of a margin turn (9.6% adjusted EBITDA) plus an
earnings beat. 🟢 Federal contract backlog of roughly $2.8–3.1B (a coverage ratio around
2.4–2.6x) and a defense-budget tailwind from the One Big Beautiful Bill. 🟢 Strong,
consistent free cash flow and a $1B buyback authorization already being used (0.4M shares
in Q2-26, $64M in Q4-25). 🟢 The revolver refinanced and upsized to 2031. 🟢 Open-market
insider buying (17 buys versus 11 sells) — the real conviction signal, distinct from the
grant-inflated ratio the screener first reported.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is disclosure architecture. The rebrand to Everforth arrives with
a reporting change ("by industry rather than mode of delivery") and a stated philosophy
that "the delivery structure of our engagement is much less meaningful than the outcomes
we drive." Read charitably, that reflects a genuine consulting pivot; read skeptically,
it reframes attention away from a staff-augmentation base that is shrinking. The Quinnox
India acquisition is explicitly a labor-cost and margin defense — offshore delivery to
counter wage and pricing deflation. And the leadership refresh is substantive: new
presidents for Commercial North America, India/International, and the Federal segment.
New voices tend to bring new baselines — often a convenient reset point for future
"growth."

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**PIVOTING.** This is a cash-generative, real franchise deliberately re-tooling itself —
toward consulting, offshore delivery and AI-enabled solutions — out of a legacy staffing
model under structural pressure. Capital allocation is rational (buybacks into weakness,
a sensible refinancing) but is being deployed against a declining revenue base.

**Moat: NARROW, and its trend is ERODING.** The Federal segment carries real switching
costs — security clearances, incumbency on multi-year contracts, and recompete advantages
(they won an FBI recompete in 2025). The Commercial segment is lower-moat, competing head
on with Accenture, the Big Four and India-based pure-plays. The width evidence points the
wrong way: return on invested capital of 7.8%, return on equity of 12.8%, and both
falling alongside four years of revenue decline and halved earnings.

**Secular threat: material (not yet terminal).** The structural force is labor-arbitrage
and AI deflation of billable IT labor — the very automation management sells to clients
also compresses the hours it can bill. This is not a business heading to zero (federal IT
and enterprise modernization are durable), but it is a slowly shrinking base, which makes
optical cheapness a value-trap risk rather than a clean bargain.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** the deep-value discount has largely closed.
The stock has run roughly 55% off its mid-July 2026 low near $17–18 (its 50-day average
is under $20) to about $28 today, on the Q2 margin-recovery print. Much of the re-rating
this thesis was meant to capture has already happened. At today's price the residual
upside to a defensible sum-of-the-parts value near the mid-$30s is modest against real
leverage and a live secular headwind. This is a stabilizing turnaround bought late, not
an unrecognized deep-value gem.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: PIVOTING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: material

2025). Over the following year that arc widened into a full re-invention: a string of
acquisitions (TopBloc and GlideFast in the Workday/ServiceNow orbit, then Quinnox for
offshore delivery in India), a bundle of new "AI accelerator" assets, a fresh senior
leadership bench, and finally a complete corporate rebrand — ASGN became Everforth in
February 2026, with the ticker moving to EFOR that April.

Two drivers were introduced with fanfare and are worth watching. First, "AI-led
transformation" became the dominant demand narrative — by the fourth-quarter 2025 call
management claimed "nearly 80% of enterprises" plan to lift AI spending in 2026. Second,
offshore India delivery (via Quinnox) was framed as the route to margin expansion. A
driver that was quietly de-emphasized: the staff-augmentation business itself. Alongside
the rebrand, management changed its commercial reporting from "mode of delivery"
(staffing versus consulting) to "by industry" — a change that, whatever its intent,
removes the very disclosure investors had used to track the decline of the legacy
staffing base.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The recurring tension is a confident bookings narrative sitting on top of a shrinking
revenue line.

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record commercial consulting bookings," book-to-bill 1.1–1.3x (every quarter) | Total revenue fell each year: $4.58B (2022) → $4.45B (2023) → $4.10B (2024) → $3.98B (2025); Q1-26 flat year on year | Bookings strength is real but is NOT converting to revenue growth — management conceded in Q1-26 that project "ramp-up time was slower than anticipated" |
| Margins "creeping up... adding to our margin profile" (Q2-25 CEO) | Adjusted EBITDA margin then MISSED in Q1-26 at 8.6%, "below our expectations"; full-year EPS collapsed from $3.83 (2024) to $2.60 (2025), and trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS is now just $1.94; net margin only 2.9% | The margin-up story broke in Q1-26 before partially healing in Q2-26 (9.6%) |
| "Disciplined capital allocation... strength of our balance sheet" | Net debt is about $1.39B against roughly $380M of adjusted EBITDA — leverage near 3.5x; the Altman-Z solvency score of 1.7 sits in the caution/distress band | The balance sheet is levered, not pristine — though they DID refinance and upsize the revolver to $600M out to 2031 (July 2026) and are buying back stock |
| AI is a demand tailwind | Revenue is still shrinking while AI adoption accelerates — the same technology that drives modernization projects also deflates the billable-labor base | Two-sided; the tailwind is real for consulting demand but does not yet offset the secular pressure on the staffing model |

The cleanest corroboration of management's better claims: free cash flow is genuine —
about $221M on a trailing-twelve-month basis, converting roughly 60–68% of EBITDA, and
Q4-25 alone produced $93.7M. This is a real cash business, not an accounting mirage.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining through 2025, then stabilizing.** Rating: Declining-to-turning.

- Q1-25: cautious but steady — management widened guidance ranges, citing "a new piece
  of news almost daily... tariffs or DOGE," framed as "just good caution."
- Q2–Q3-25: the most offensive tone of the window — "AI is not merely a passing fad but a
  fundamental replatforming," record commercial bookings, the One Big Beautiful Bill
  defense-budget tailwind.
- Q4-25/Q1-26: distinctly defensive — "very volatile macro environment," "disciplined
  expense management," and the admission of an EBITDA-margin miss. The language shifted
  from growth and investment toward cost control and "strengthening our foundation."
- Q2-26 (July): a modest confidence rebound on the earnings beat and margin recovery.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** Management is reliable on the top line and less so on margin. Through 2025
revenue repeatedly landed "at" or "above the high end" of guidance, and Q2-26 revenue and
EPS both beat consensus (EPS $0.91 versus $0.81 expected). But the Q1-26 adjusted-EBITDA
margin of 8.6% came in below management's own expectation — a genuine miss on the metric
that matters most to this thesis. The screener's beat rate of four of the last seven
quarters (57%) is consistent with a "usually hits, occasionally stumbles" profile. No
strong sandbagging pattern; if anything the margin guide has been slightly optimistic.
Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Two questions recur and are never fully put to bed. Surinder Thind (of the sell side)
pressed quarter after quarter on the true go-forward margin run-rate and on financial-
services weakness — and in Q1-26 that pressure was vindicated when margins missed. Mark
Marcon repeatedly probed whether the margin compression reflected pricing pressure or
mere mix; management insisted "we're not seeing a material compression in pricing... it
was really timing" and "mix." That deflection is the single most important claim to
distrust: if the softness is structural pricing rather than temporary mix, the recovery
management promises "gradually throughout the year, won't rubber-band it" may not arrive.
Marcon also pushed on days-sales-outstanding and free-cash-flow conversion; management
attributed it to seasonality with "no change in behavior, no increase in bad debt."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Revenue has declined four consecutive years and earnings per share have more than
halved from the 2022 peak. 🔴 The Q1-26 margin miss, with federal book-to-bill sliding to
0.7x that quarter. 🔴 Leverage near 3.5x with an Altman-Z of 1.7. 🔴 Analyst price-target
velocity is down about 37% versus the year-ago average, and a plaintiff law firm
(Johnson Fistel) publicized a securities-law "investigation" in May 2026 — boilerplate
that follows any large drawdown, but worth noting. 🔴 The reporting change that hides the
staffing-versus-consulting split.

🟢 Q2-26 delivered the first hard evidence of a margin turn (9.6% adjusted EBITDA) plus an
earnings beat. 🟢 Federal contract backlog of roughly $2.8–3.1B (a coverage ratio around
2.4–2.6x) and a defense-budget tailwind from the One Big Beautiful Bill. 🟢 Strong,
consistent free cash flow and a $1B buyback authorization already being used (0.4M shares
in Q2-26, $64M in Q4-25). 🟢 The revolver refinanced and upsized to 2031. 🟢 Open-market
insider buying (17 buys versus 11 sells) — the real conviction signal, distinct from the
grant-inflated ratio the screener first reported.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is disclosure architecture. The rebrand to Everforth arrives with
a reporting change ("by industry rather than mode of delivery") and a stated philosophy
that "the delivery structure of our engagement is much less meaningful than the outcomes
we drive." Read charitably, that reflects a genuine consulting pivot; read skeptically,
it reframes attention away from a staff-augmentation base that is shrinking. The Quinnox
India acquisition is explicitly a labor-cost and margin defense — offshore delivery to
counter wage and pricing deflation. And the leadership refresh is substantive: new
presidents for Commercial North America, India/International, and the Federal segment.
New voices tend to bring new baselines — often a convenient reset point for future
"growth."

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**PIVOTING.** This is a cash-generative, real franchise deliberately re-tooling itself —
toward consulting, offshore delivery and AI-enabled solutions — out of a legacy staffing
model under structural pressure. Capital allocation is rational (buybacks into weakness,
a sensible refinancing) but is being deployed against a declining revenue base.

**Moat: NARROW, and its trend is ERODING.** The Federal segment carries real switching
costs — security clearances, incumbency on multi-year contracts, and recompete advantages
(they won an FBI recompete in 2025). The Commercial segment is lower-moat, competing head
on with Accenture, the Big Four and India-based pure-plays. The width evidence points the
wrong way: return on invested capital of 7.8%, return on equity of 12.8%, and both
falling alongside four years of revenue decline and halved earnings.

**Secular threat: material (not yet terminal).** The structural force is labor-arbitrage
and AI deflation of billable IT labor — the very automation management sells to clients
also compresses the hours it can bill. This is not a business heading to zero (federal IT
and enterprise modernization are durable), but it is a slowly shrinking base, which makes
optical cheapness a value-trap risk rather than a clean bargain.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** the deep-value discount has largely closed.
The stock has run roughly 55% off its mid-July 2026 low near $17–18 (its 50-day average
is under $20) to about $28 today, on the Q2 margin-recovery print. Much of the re-rating
this thesis was meant to capture has already happened. At today's price the residual
upside to a defensible sum-of-the-parts value near the mid-$30s is modest against real
leverage and a live secular headwind. This is a stabilizing turnaround bought late, not
an unrecognized deep-value gem.
